passage_text: Researchers at the Cognitive Neuroscience Laboratory investigated how brief mindfulness training affects reaction times in a simple visual detection task. Forty healthy adults (age 20–35) were randomly assigned to one of four groups of 10 participants each. The mindfulness group received a 10‑minute guided meditation before each of the 20 trials. The control group listened to a neutral audio clip. The placebo group received a 10‑minute sham guided exercise, presented as meditation but without mindfulness instructions. The no‑intervention group began each trial with no preceding activity. Reaction times (RTs) were recorded in milliseconds. Table 1 summarizes the mean RTs and standard deviations for each group. The results suggest that mindfulness training may reduce RTs, but the variability within groups also differs. These findings raise questions about the mechanisms underlying the observed effects and whether the benefits are consistent across individuals.
stem: Which group had the highest mean reaction time?
explanation: The table shows the No Intervention group with a mean RT of 420 ms, higher than all other groups.
trap: Choosing Control because of its name instead of comparing all four means.

stem: Which experimental design would best test whether the observed difference in mean reaction times is caused by the mindfulness intervention?
explanation: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) randomly assigns participants to intervention or control, controlling for confounding variables and establishing causality.
trap: Choosing a cohort study because participants are observed over trials, ignoring that only random assignment supports causal claims.

stem: What is the pooled standard deviation for the Mindfulness and Control groups (n=10 each)?
explanation: Correct: With equal n, pooled SD = sqrt((45² + 60²)/2) = sqrt(2812.5) ≈ 53 ms. Why the others are wrong: A) 45 is only the Mindfulness group SD. C) 60 is only the Control group SD. D) 70 exceeds both SDs; a pooled SD must lie between them.
trap: Using one group's SD, or a sum/other value that falls outside the range of the two SDs.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?

options.A: The Mindfulness group had the lowest mean reaction time of the four groups.
options.B: The Control group had higher variability than the No Intervention group.
options.C: The Placebo group had a lower mean reaction time than the Control group.
options.D: The No Intervention group had the highest mean reaction time.

explanation: Correct: The Control SD (60 ms) is lower than the No Intervention SD (65 ms), so the Control group did not have higher variability. Why the others are wrong: A) 350 ms is lower than 410, 395 and 420 ms. C) 395 ms (Placebo) is lower than 410 ms (Control). D) 420 ms is the highest of the four means.
trap: Misreading which of 60 and 65 is larger when comparing variability.

stem: The researchers want to attribute the lower reaction time to mindfulness meditation itself rather than to expectation or listening to audio. Which comparison in Table 1 is most relevant?

options.D: The SDs of the Control and No Intervention groups

explanation: Correct: The Placebo group received a sham exercise presented as meditation, so Mindfulness (350 ms) versus Placebo (395 ms) isolates the effect of the mindfulness content. Why the others are wrong: A) neither group involves mindfulness, so it cannot isolate its effect. C) neither group involves mindfulness, so it cannot isolate its effect. D) variability comparisons say nothing about the cause of the mean difference.
trap: Picking a comparison that does not include the mindfulness group.
